Myers (Chionodraco myersi) attains a maximum total length of 39.2 centimeters [Li = 39.2 centimeters], a size that situates it among the larger members of the Antarctic icefish family Channichthyidae. Field surveys in the Ross Sea have consistently recorded gravid females measuring between 35 and 40 centimeters, with the ultimate total length representing the upper asymptote of the species growth trajectory. This elongated, fusiform body plan is typical of pelagic notothenioids, enabling efficient cruising through the frigid, oxygen-rich waters of the Southern Ocean, where temperatures hover near -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C]. The length-weight relationship derived from trawl-caught specimens indicates that an individual nearing this maximum length would achieve an ultimate wet weight of approximately 405 grams [Wwi = approximately 405 grams], a value obtained through the power-law equation commonly applied to channichthyid fishes. This relatively modest body mass, despite the substantial length, reflects the reduced ossification and low muscle density characteristic of the family, adaptations that reduce the energetic cost of buoyancy regulation in a pelagic existence.

The onset of sexual maturation in Chionodraco myersi is marked by the attainment of a total length at puberty of 27.55 centimeters [Lp = 27.55 centimeters], a threshold estimated by scaling the known puberty length of the congener Chionodraco hamatus to account for the larger ultimate size of C. myersi. Juveniles undergoing gonadal recrudescence at this length transition from a strictly foraging existence to one that includes the metabolic demands of gametogenesis. At puberty, an individual typically weighs approximately 120 grams [Wwp = approximately 120 grams], derived from the same length-mass allometry that predicts adult asymptotic mass. This shift represents a significant physiological milestone, as the fish must allocate resources toward both continued somatic expansion and the development of reproductive tissues. Comparison with other channichthyids suggests that the Lp-to-Li ratio in C. myersi is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes delayed reproduction in favor of achieving a larger body size, a pattern frequently observed in high-latitude fishes facing extreme seasonal food limitation.

Reproductive investment in Myers is tightly constrained by the persistently low environmental temperatures of the Antarctic continental shelf, where water temperature remains at -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C] throughout the year. Under these thermal conditions, newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal eggs weighing just 0.0335 grams [Wwb = 0.0335 grams] at birth, a mass derived from the estimated egg diameter of 3.8 to 4.2 millimeters using the volume formula for a sphere. The extreme cold slows every physiological process, and the encapsulated embryo requires an incubation period of approximately 85 days [ab = approximately 85 days] before chorion rupture and yolk-sac larva eclosion at a temperature of -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C]. This extended developmental window, in turn, constrains the species maximum reproductive rate, which has been estimated at a fecundity of 6,200 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 6,200 eggs per clutch] and a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], reflecting a continuous spawning strategy over the austral summer. The larvae emerge at a point when the brief seasonal bloom of phytoplankton and copepods provides the first exogenous food sources, but the narrow temporal window for successful recruitment imposes a critical bottleneck on population replenishment.

Long-term mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimates indicate that Chionodraco myersi individuals reach a maximum lifespan of approximately 6,570 days [am = approximately 6,570 days] under the prevailing conditions of the Ross Sea, where water temperature is maintained at -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C]. This longevity, translating to about 18 years [am = about 18 years], is remarkably extended for a teleost of its body size and stands in stark contrast to the short-lived, fast-growing life histories of temperate and tropical fishes. at a temperature of -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C]The protracted lifespan reflects the profoundly low metabolic rates enforced by the polar thermal regime; cellular damage accumulates slowly, and senescence-related mortality is correspondingly delayed. Field observations of recaptured individuals bearing tags applied over a decade earlier confirm that adults maintain stable body condition and continue to participate in spawning aggregations well into their second decade. This life-history strategy, combining slow growth, late maturation, and extreme longevity, is a common evolutionary response to the severe seasonality and low productivity of the Southern Ocean ecosystem, where reproductive opportunities are infrequent and unpredictable.

Females of Chionodraco myersi produce a single clutch of demersal eggs each year, and the maximum reproductive output of 6,200 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 6,200 eggs per clutch] combined with one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year] reflects the constraints imposed by the species slow metabolic pace at -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C]. The energetic cost of vitellogenesis is substantial, requiring the mobilization of lipid reserves accumulated during the preceding summer foraging season, and the egg diameter of 3.8 to 4.2 millimeters is among the largest recorded for any notothenioid, ensuring that the prolarva emerges with sufficient yolk to sustain it through the critical first weeks of exogenous feeding. This spawning strategy aligns with the slow pace of life typical of polar fishes, where the brief summer productivity window dictates that each reproductive event must be relatively large to offset the high larval mortality imposed by the unpredictable environment.
